text: SOC 2 and ISO 27001 are things a company chooses to pursue to demonstrate trustworthiness. PCI DSS and HIPAA work completely differently — they apply because of what data an organization actually touches, not because it opted in. Getting that applicability question wrong, in either direction, is expensive: either a real compliance violation, or security spend poured into controls you never actually needed.

PCI DSS applies to any organization that stores, processes, or transmits cardholder data, and the single most consequential question in any assessment is scope — specifically, the Cardholder Data Environment, the people, process, and technology that touch card data or could affect its security. A huge amount of real PCI work is actually scope reduction: isolating that environment and routing checkout through a validated third-party processor so your own systems never see a raw card number at all.

HIPAA is U.S. federal law, and it turns on two roles. A covered entity is a health plan, clearinghouse, or provider. A business associate is a vendor that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits Protected Health Information on behalf of one — a hosting provider, a billing company, an analytics vendor with patient-data access. PHI itself is individually identifiable health information: a name next to a lab result, a record number, even an appointment tied to someone's identity.

The legal hinge that actually creates the obligation is the Business Associate Agreement — a required contract spelling out how PHI gets protected, used only for permitted purposes, and reported if breached. A vendor that never touches PHI, even serving healthcare clients, may not need one at all. A vendor that does touch PHI without a BAA in place has a real, independently sanctionable gap, no matter how strong its technical controls otherwise are.

The lesson underneath both frameworks is the same: the trigger is the data, not the industry label, and documenting that determination is itself real compliance work. Next lesson pulls this together with the practice that makes all of this manageable at scale — mapping one well-designed control, like access control, so it satisfies requirements across SOC 2, ISO 27001, and PCI DSS at the same time, instead of building separate control sets for each.
